hoy.t: The lead story: MarketWatch reports “Nowhere to hide: Tech selloff hits software and chip stocks alike”. Also on the page: Bitcoin price line, Strait of Hormuz traffic, 2026 midterms (House control) and US CPI (September print).
What moved: The NAOS dollar index fell 0.4% on 16 Oct (ECB). The US 2-year yield fell 3 bp to 4.74% on 16 Oct (U.S. Treasury).

What the markets say: Polymarket shows Bitcoin above $82,000 on Oct 18 is 30% likely; Polymarket shows Hormuz traffic is back to normal by Dec 31 is 12% likely (11:48 UTC). Prices set by traders, not NAOS forecasts.
In one room: the CoinDesk headline uses “bitcoin”, a word NAOS files under “Bitcoin price line”, so its room shows bitcoin's move, that market's odds of Bitcoin above $82,000 on Oct 18.

ia.titulo: Nowhere to hide: Tech selloff hits software and chip stocks alike

texto: Bitcoin is down 0.04% since 00:00 UTC and up 0.5% over 30 days.
In the past month its typical daily move was about 0.7%, so today is a quiet day so far.

What this is: one day's price change on CoinGecko's market feed. What this is not: a forecast. A month of gains or losses says little about the next month, and bitcoin has often swung 10% or more within a few weeks.
On 16 Oct the 10-year Treasury yield was 0.35 percentage points above the 2-year, so the curve is positive, the usual shape. In the last 90 days it stayed between 0.20 and 0.53 points.

What it has meant before: an inverted curve came before most US recessions since the late 1960s, usually by about 6 to 24 months, and it has also given false alarms. In past cycles the curve often turned positive again shortly before a recession began, so a positive curve on its own is no all-clear.

What it means for people: the 2-year (4.74%) follows what markets expect from the Fed over the next two years, and US mortgage and other long loan rates tend to follow the 10-year (5.09%). Together they set the tone for borrowing costs over the coming months.
